title: SQL
summary: Ask questions of data: SELECT, filtering, joins and aggregates on a live SQLite database.

lessons.title: SQL: syntax basics

concept.text:
SQL (Structured Query Language) is how you talk to a relational database. Data lives in **tables** made of rows and columns, like a spreadsheet with strict rules.

You describe **what** you want, not how to get it. `SELECT name FROM students WHERE grade > 80` reads almost like a sentence, and the database works out the fastest way to answer.
concept.analogy: A database is a huge filing room and SQL is the request slip you hand the clerk: which cabinet (FROM), which folders (WHERE), and which pages to photocopy (SELECT).

visual.caption: The order the database actually processes a query.

steps.title: Select columns
steps.text: `*` means every column. Naming columns is clearer and faster.

steps.title: Filter rows
steps.text: Text values use single quotes. Combine conditions with AND and OR.
steps.code: SELECT name FROM students WHERE city = 'Austin' AND grade >= 85;

steps.title: Sort and limit
steps.code: SELECT name, grade FROM students ORDER BY grade DESC LIMIT 2;

steps.title: Change data
steps.text: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes them, DELETE removes them. Always include WHERE on UPDATE and DELETE, or every row is affected.
steps.code:
INSERT INTO students (name, grade, city) VALUES ('Eli', 88, 'Boston');
UPDATE students SET grade = 80 WHERE name = 'Ben';

interactive.seed: CREATE TABLE students(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, grade INTEGER, city TEXT); INSERT INTO students(name, grade, city) VALUES ('Ava',91,'Austin'),('Ben',78,'Boston'),('Cy',85,'Austin'),('Dee',62,'Denver'),('Eve',95,'Boston');

challenge.prompt: List the names and cities of the two lowest-scoring students who are **not** from Denver.
challenge.hint: Use `WHERE city != 'Denver'`, sort ascending by grade, and `LIMIT 2`.
challenge.seed: CREATE TABLE students(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, grade INTEGER, city TEXT); INSERT INTO students(name, grade, city) VALUES ('Ava',91,'Austin'),('Ben',78,'Boston'),('Cy',85,'Austin'),('Dee',62,'Denver'),('Eve',95,'Boston');
challenge.starter:
SELECT name, city
FROM students
-- finish the query
;
challenge.solution:
SELECT name, city
FROM students
WHERE city != 'Denver'
ORDER BY grade ASC
LIMIT 2;
-- Ben (Boston), Cy (Austin)

takeaways: Tables hold rows and columns. SELECT reads, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE write.
WHERE filters rows, ORDER BY sorts, LIMIT caps the count.
Never run UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause.

lessons.title: SQL: joins, grouping and keys

concept.text:
Real databases split data across tables to avoid repeating it. A **primary key** uniquely identifies each row, and a **foreign key** in another table points back to it. A **JOIN** stitches the tables together at query time.

**GROUP BY** collapses many rows into one per group so you can count, sum or average them.
concept.analogy: A join is matching name tags. One table lists guests with badge numbers, another lists badge numbers with meal choices. Line up the badge numbers and you know who is eating what.

visual.caption: The joins you will actually use.
rows: Only rows that match in both tables
Every left row, plus matches (or NULL)
You must not lose left rows, e.g. students with no club

steps.title: Join two tables
steps.text: `ON` says which columns must match. Short aliases (s, c) keep it readable.

steps.title: Keep unmatched rows
steps.text: A LEFT JOIN keeps students with no club. Their club column is NULL.

steps.title: Aggregate
steps.text: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX summarise each group.

steps.title: Filter groups
steps.text: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after.

interactive.seed: CREATE TABLE students(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, grade INTEGER, city TEXT); INSERT INTO students(name, grade, city) VALUES ('Ava',91,'Austin'),('Ben',78,'Boston'),('Cy',85,'Austin'),('Dee',62,'Denver'),('Eve',95,'Boston'); CREATE TABLE clubs(student_id INTEGER REFERENCES students(id), club TEXT); INSERT INTO clubs VALUES (1,'Chess'),(1,'Robotics'),(3,'Chess'),(5,'Robotics');
interactive.starter:
-- Tables: students(id, name, grade, city) and clubs(student_id, club)
SELECT s.name, c.club
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN clubs c ON c.student_id = s.id;

SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS students, ROUND(AVG(grade), 1) AS avg_grade
FROM students
GROUP BY city
ORDER BY avg_grade DESC;

challenge.prompt: Show each club with its number of members and the average grade of those members, highest average first.
challenge.hint: Join clubs to students, then `GROUP BY c.club`.
challenge.seed: CREATE TABLE students(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, grade INTEGER, city TEXT); INSERT INTO students(name, grade, city) VALUES ('Ava',91,'Austin'),('Ben',78,'Boston'),('Cy',85,'Austin'),('Dee',62,'Denver'),('Eve',95,'Boston'); CREATE TABLE clubs(student_id INTEGER REFERENCES students(id), club TEXT); INSERT INTO clubs VALUES (1,'Chess'),(1,'Robotics'),(3,'Chess'),(5,'Robotics');
challenge.starter:
SELECT c.club
FROM clubs c
-- finish the query
;
challenge.solution:
SELECT c.club, COUNT(*) AS members, AVG(s.grade) AS avg_grade
FROM clubs c
JOIN students s ON s.id = c.student_id
GROUP BY c.club
ORDER BY avg_grade DESC;
-- Robotics 2 93.0, Chess 2 88.0

takeaways: Primary keys identify rows. Foreign keys link tables.
INNER JOIN keeps matches only. LEFT JOIN keeps every left-hand row.
GROUP BY plus an aggregate answers 'how many per…' questions.

lessons.title: SQL mini project: a small shop database

concept.text: You will design a schema for a shop, load data and answer business questions. Designing the tables is the real skill: each fact should be stored once, in one place. That principle is called normalisation.
concept.analogy: Storing a customer's address on every order is like writing your phone number on every page of a notebook. Change it once and all the other pages are wrong. Keep it on one page and point to it.

visual.caption: How the three tables link together.

steps.title: Create the tables
steps.text: Each table gets an integer primary key. The orders table holds two foreign keys.

steps.title: Insert data
steps.text: Insert parents (customers, products) before children (orders) so the references exist.

steps.title: Answer questions
steps.text: Revenue per customer needs both joins: orders to customers for the name, orders to products for the price.

challenge.prompt: Add a query to the editor above that lists customers who have **never** placed an order.
challenge.hint: LEFT JOIN customers to orders, then keep rows where the order side is NULL.
challenge.solution:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
-- Cy

takeaways: Store each fact once and link tables with keys.
Multi-table questions are chains of joins followed by GROUP BY.
LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL finds rows with no match.
